---
title: "tscv_in_R"
format: html
editor: visual
---

Install needed libraries. More specifically, the fable package since that will include the models we will use, and the fable table output that we get.

```{r}
library(tsibble)
library(fable)
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)
library(tsibbledata)
library(glue)
```

Here, we set our horizon to 4. So we want to forecast 4 months into the future. INIT is our training window of 240 months or 20 years.

```{r}
# Maximum number of forecast horizons
H <- 4
# First origin: 20 years of monthly data
INIT <- 240

# Filter for the specific series: Victoria restaurant sales
cafes <- aus_retail |>
  filter(
    State == "Victoria",
    Industry == "Cafes, restaurants and catering services"
  )

head(cafes)
```

Lets see the whole time series length in both months and years.

```{r}
total_months <- select(cafes, Month) |> nrow()
total_years <- total_months / 12 
cat(glue("Total months in dataset: {total_months}"))
cat(glue("Total years covered: {total_years}"))

cat(glue("Here is our training size percentage: "))
cat(glue("Training: {INIT}"))
cat(glue("RATIO: {INIT} / {total_months} = %{INIT / total_months}"))
```

Lets create the expanding window tsibble. It will return to us each window as a row entry in the resulting table.

```{r}
origins_expand <- cafes |>
  stretch_tsibble(.init = INIT, .step = 1)


head(origins_expand)
```

Lets compare the difference in column names now. The .id represents what window that month belongs to (.id is a key). The window was defined in INIT.

```{r}
cat(glue("{colnames(cafes)}"))
cat(glue("{colnames(origins_expand)}"))
```

Lets use the four benchmark models on EACH window.

MEAN - mean model SNAIVE - Seasonal naïve method RW - Random walk with drift (often just “the drift method”) TSLM - Time series linear model, a linear regression

Each one of these will produce a forecast for each window for horizon months 1, 2, 3, and 4 into the future.

```{r}
tscv_expand_fc <- origins_expand |>
  model(mean = MEAN(Turnover),
        snaive = SNAIVE(Turnover),
        drift = RW(Turnover ~ drift()),
        tslm = TSLM(Turnover ~ trend() + season())) |>
  forecast(h = H) |>
  filter(Month <= max(cafes$Month)) |>
  group_by(.id, .model) |> mutate(h = row_number()) |> ungroup() |>
  as_fable(response = "Turnover", distribution = Turnover)

head(tscv_expand_fc)
```

We want an actual fable. So we transform this table into what we need.

The steps:

1.  For each forecast, compute the error: actual − forecast.
2.  Take the absolute value, so overestimates and underestimates both count as positive.
3.  Average those absolute errors for each model and each horizon, pooling across all the windows.

```{r}

# USES MEAN ABSOLUTE ERROR

acc_expand <- tscv_expand_fc |>
  accuracy(cafes, by = c("h", ".model")) |>
  select(h, .model, MAE) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = .model, values_from = c(MAE)) #|>
  #kable(digits = 2, caption = "MAE by Model and Horizon")

head(acc_expand)

```

So this uses MAE ("Mean absolute error"). It looks at the forecast made for each model, then the actual observed value. It takes the \|observed - forecast\| and then sums up that value at each window and divides by total windows. This just gives you the average at each horizon for each model.

# MAE = (sum of \|observed − forecast\| over all windows) ÷ (number of forecasts)

Lets plot how each model did.

```{r}
library(ggplot2)

fc_h1 <- tscv_expand_fc |>
  filter(h == 1) |>
  as_tibble()

ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = cafes, aes(x = Month, y = Turnover),
            colour = "black", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(data = fc_h1, aes(x = Month, y = .mean, colour = .model)) +
  labs(x = "Month", y = "Turnover ($M AUD)", colour = "Model",
       title = "1-month-ahead forecasts vs actual turnover")
```

```{r}

ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = cafes |> filter(Month >= min(fc_h1$Month)),
            aes(x = Month, y = Turnover), colour = "black", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(data = fc_h1, aes(x = Month, y = .mean, colour = .model)) +
  labs(x = "Month", y = "Turnover ($M AUD)", colour = "Model")

```

Now lets try a sliding/rolling window. This difference here is that it discards old information when making the calculation.

-   Expanding window (stretch_tsibble()): starts at the first observation every time, so each training set includes all data up to the forecast origin.

-   Rolling window (slide_tsibble()): fixed length, say 240 months. Each time a new month is added, the oldest one drops out.

```{r}
H <- 4 # same horizon
WIN <- 240 # our window size

origins_roll <- cafes |>
  slide_tsibble(.size = WIN, .step = 1)

head(origins_roll)

```

Same steps as before for setting up the fable. Does identical work. Just using rolling window instead. 

```{r}

tscv_rolling_fc <- origins_roll |>
  model(mean = MEAN(Turnover),
        snaive = SNAIVE(Turnover),
        drift = RW(Turnover ~ drift()),
        tslm = TSLM(Turnover ~ trend() + season())) |>
  forecast(h = H) |>
  filter(Month <= max(cafes$Month)) |>
  group_by(.id, .model) |> mutate(h = row_number()) |> ungroup() |>
  as_fable(response = "Turnover", distribution = Turnover)

head(tscv_rolling_fc)

```

Lets get the same MAE data we did before, but now on the rolling window instead. 

```{r}

# USES MEAN ABSOLUTE ERROR

acc_rolling <- tscv_rolling_fc |>
  accuracy(cafes, by = c("h", ".model")) |>
  select(h, .model, MAE) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = .model, values_from = c(MAE)) #|>
  #kable(digits = 2, caption = "MAE by Model and Horizon")

head(acc_rolling)


```
In general, the rolling window does a lot better. The most obvious example is the differences in the MAE of the mean models. Lets compare. 

```{r}

expanding_mean <- acc_expand  |> select(h, expanding = mean)
rolling_mean   <- acc_rolling |> select(h, rolling = mean)

compare_means <- inner_join(expanding_mean, rolling_mean, by = "h")
compare_means

```
Lets just see the differences between all of the model errors for both expanding and rolling. 

```{r}
compare_model_errors <- inner_join(acc_expand, acc_rolling, by = "h",
                                   suffix = c("_expanding", "_rolling")) 

compare_model_errors
```
Lets take the differences and we can get a better idea since theres a lot going on in the table above. Not as easily readable. 

```{r}

diff_errors <- inner_join(
  acc_expand  |> pivot_longer(-h, names_to = "model", values_to = "expanding"),
  acc_rolling |> pivot_longer(-h, names_to = "model", values_to = "rolling"),
  by = c("h", "model")
) |>
  mutate(diff = rolling - expanding) |> # do rolling - expanding here! rolling has the lower error
  select(h, model, diff) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = model, values_from = diff)

diff_errors
```
Negative means the rolling window had lower error which means better forecasting accuracy. Positive means the expanding window did better.The SNAIVE model had a difference of zero? So they the performance is the same regardless of whether or not its rolling or expanding?
